lane.name: Molina and the Magnolia circle
lane.definition: Jason Molina's projects (Songs: Ohia, Magnolia Electric Co., solo) and the Secretly Canadian / Will Johnson orbit: haunted folk that grew into Crazy Horse-scale country rock.

albums.label: Steve Records
albums.description: Will Johnson's debut full-length as Centro-matic is scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar rock cut fast and cheap. It sounds like a home-recorded garage band with a country streak rather than a polished studio act, closer to lo-fi indie rock than to alt-country proper. It marks the start of the prolific Denton output that Centro-matic and South San Gabriel would build out over the next two decades.
albums.lineage: Launches Will Johnson's Centro-matic and, with it, the Denton, Texas wing of the Molina/Magnolia orbit.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Released the same year as the Songs: Ohia debut, this early EP collects spare, plainly recorded songs like 'Pass' and 'Defenders' that feel closer to sketches than finished songs. It shares the debut's stark voice-and-guitar sound and dark, allusive titles. It is a minor, early document more than a destination record, useful mainly for hearing how quickly Molina was already writing and releasing material.
albums.lineage: A same-year companion to the Songs: Ohia debut LP, part of the flood of early Secretly Canadian releases that established Molina's stark solo sound before the full band arrived.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Jason Molina's debut as Songs: Ohia, nicknamed 'the Black Album' for its plain dark sleeve, is little more than his high, reverb-soaked voice and a spare guitar, cut fast and plainly. The songs sit over almost no percussion, just repeated, incantatory phrases about ghosts, rivers and the Midwestern dark. It set the stark, haunted template Molina returned to for the rest of his career.
albums.lineage: Molina's first single came out on Will Oldham's Palace Records, and this album sounds kin to the same lo-fi, DIY folk underground; it established the voice-and-guitar minimalism that later Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co. records built from or reacted against.

albums.label: Happy Go Lucky
albums.description: Molina's second Songs: Ohia LP keeps the rough, homemade feel of the debut but lets a looser, shifting cast of players clatter behind him, giving songs like 'An Ace Unable to Change' a more unsettled pulse. The songs drift between hushed voice-and-guitar pieces and ramshackle band takes, with titles that hint at a private mythology. It is rougher and more obscure than the albums that followed, a transitional record between bedroom tape and full-band songwriter.
albums.lineage: Bridges the stripped-down debut and the fuller-band Axxess & Ace, part of Molina's rapid early run of Secretly Canadian-adjacent releases out of the Bloomington/Chicago underground.
key_tracks: This Time Anything Finite at All

albums.label: Idol Records
albums.description: Centro-matic's second album thickens the fuzz-guitar rock of the debut with more developed arrangements while keeping Johnson's frayed, unpolished vocal delivery up front. The songs still sound cut live and fast, prioritizing feel over finish. It shows Centro-matic edging from lo-fi noise-rock toward the more country-inflected sound of their 2000s records.
albums.lineage: Continues Centro-matic's fast, fuzz-heavy development toward the fuller alt-country/Crazy Horse sound of 'Distance and Clime' and 'Love You Just the Same'.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Axxess & Ace tightens Molina's songwriting into something closer to conventional verse-chorus structure while keeping the hushed, echo-drenched production of his earliest work. 'Captain Badass' stretches out as a slow-burning centerpiece, while 'Love & Work' and 'Redhead' show a plainer, more direct kind of heartbreak song. It is the record where Molina's songwriting starts to catch up with his atmosphere, and a good first stop for newcomers.
albums.lineage: Continues the Secretly Canadian run that runs from Songs: Ohia's debut through The Lioness, tightening the songwriting that would fully bloom on Didn't It Rain and Magnolia Electric Co.

albums.album: All the Falsest Hearts Can Try
albums.label: Quality Park/Munich Records
albums.description: Released on the Netherlands-based Munich label, this album keeps pace with Centro-matic's rapid-fire recording habits, another set of scuffed-up, guitar-forward rock songs built around Will Johnson's plainspoken drawl. The same fuzzed, Crazy Horse-tilted core of their celebrated 2000s records is already in place. It underlines how prolifically Centro-matic worked in their first Denton decade.
albums.lineage: One of several rapid-fire early Centro-matic releases building the fuzz-guitar, alt-country sound the band would refine through the 2000s.
key_tracks: Cool That You Showed Us How

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Ghost Tropic is the slowest and most drone-like Songs: Ohia record, built from long, barely-moving pieces like 'Not Just a Ghost's Heart' and 'Incantation.' Molina's guitar and voice sit in wide, reverberant space with sparse percussion rather than pushing toward a chorus, closer to American slowcore than to a folk or country record. It is for patient listeners who want Molina at his most spectral.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Low- and Codeine-style slowcore more than any other Songs: Ohia record, sitting between the folk-noir of The Lioness and the gospel-country turn of Didn't It Rain.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: A solo, mostly acoustic album sold at live shows, Protection Spells is one of Molina's least-heard records, closer in spirit to the stark debut than to the full-band records surrounding it. The songs are recorded plainly, voice and guitar with little else, slow and hushed. It is a tour artifact for committed fans rather than a starting point.
albums.lineage: A between-albums tour-only release from the same 2000 stretch that produced The Lioness and Ghost Tropic, showing the stripped-down solo mode Molina kept returning to between full-band records.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Recorded in Scotland with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap, The Lioness pairs Molina's voice with a chillier, more atmospheric backing than his American records, opening on the slow drone of 'The Black Crow.' Songs like 'Lioness' and 'Tigress' move at a near-funereal pace, closer to Scottish folk-noir than to Americana. It is one of the clearest points of contact between the Songs: Ohia catalog and the Drag City/Will Oldham circle, via Roberts.
albums.lineage: Made with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap in Scotland, linking the Songs: Ohia catalog directly to the UK folk underground that also produced Roberts's own records.

albums.label: Idol/Munich
albums.description: Will Johnson's quieter alter-ego project to Centro-matic, South San Gabriel's debut was originally released under the Centro-matic name before Johnson split his catalog into a loud band and a hushed one. Sparse, slow, and largely acoustic, it points toward the slowcore-adjacent side of the Denton scene rather than Centro-matic's fuzzed-out rock. It is the origin point of a project Johnson would keep alive alongside Centro-matic for another decade.
albums.lineage: Splits off from Centro-matic as Will Johnson's hushed, slow-tempo alter ego, establishing a quieter parallel track to the Crazy Horse fuzz of his main band.

albums.label: Idol/Munich
albums.description: Centro-matic's fourth full-length pushes the band's fuzzed-out guitar rock into longer, more patient arrangements, trading some of the earlier records' scrappiness for a fuller, more deliberate sound. Will Johnson's songwriting stays plainspoken and drawled, but the band -- now a steadier four-piece with Scott Danbom and Mark Hedman -- plays with more room to stretch out. It sits at the midpoint between Centro-matic's lo-fi 1990s records and the more assured 'Love You Just the Same'.
albums.lineage: Marks Centro-matic settling into its core lineup (Johnson, Pence, Danbom, Hedman), the same band that would carry through 'Love You Just the Same' and 'Fort Recovery'.

albums.album: Mi Sei Apparso Come Un Fantasma
albums.label: Paper Cup
albums.description: Recorded live in Italy and released there by a small label, this set captures the full-band version of Songs: Ohia on the road, reworking songs like 'Tigress' and 'Being in Love' from The Lioness alongside looser, newer material. It is louder and more electric than the studio records of the same period, with longer, looser arrangements. It documents the road band rather than making a studio statement.
albums.lineage: A snapshot of the touring Songs: Ohia band, showing how the sound opened up once Molina had a full electric group behind him, pointing toward Didn't It Rain and The Magnolia Electric Co.

albums.label: Galaxia
albums.description: A one-off project pairing Jason Molina with Will Oldham and Scotland's Alasdair Roberts, this is plain, unplugged folk balladry, closer to a front-porch song-swap than any of the three writers' main bands. Tracks like 'Maa Bonny Lad' and 'The Gypsy He-Witch' lean on traditional-sounding melodies and close, unpolished harmonies. It is a minor but telling document of how tightly the Molina and Will Oldham/Drag City circles overlapped.
albums.lineage: Directly links Jason Molina to Will Oldham's Drag City deadpan-folk lineage (V2) through a shared acoustic side-project with Alasdair Roberts.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Recorded in Philadelphia with members of the bluegrass band Jim & Jennie & the Pinetops, Didn't It Rain trades Ghost Tropic's dense drone for a warmer, near-gospel small-group sound. The title track and 'Blue Factory Flame' stretch out on repeated, mantra-like phrases over sparse drums and hushed harmony vocals. It feels like the true beginning of the Magnolia Electric Co. sound, a year before the name change, and is a natural first Molina record.
albums.lineage: The field guide's other suggested starting point alongside Magnolia Electric Co.; its gospel-tinged small-band sound is the direct bridge from the earlier solo Songs: Ohia records to the full-band Crazy Horse-scale group that followed.

albums.label: Undertow
albums.description: Will Johnson's first solo album, released while Centro-matic was still active, strips his songwriting down to just voice and acoustic guitar, closer to a demo tape than a full-band record. It is quieter and more intimate than either Centro-matic or South San Gabriel, letting his weathered, plainspoken vocal carry the whole record. It set the pattern for Johnson's parallel solo career alongside his main bands.
albums.lineage: Opens Will Johnson's solo catalog, a stripped-down extension of the same Denton songwriting that fed Centro-matic and South San Gabriel.

albums.label: Misra/Munich
albums.description: 'Love You Just the Same' balances big, fuzzed-out guitar rockers like 'Mighty Midshipman' with quieter, more melodic turns. Will Johnson's voice is as ragged as ever, but the band's arrangements are tighter and more confident than on the 1990s records. It is a strong entry point for the Centro-matic side of the Molina/Magnolia orbit.
albums.lineage: Represents the fully formed Denton version of Centro-matic's Crazy Horse-indebted country rock, sounding like a sibling to Magnolia Electric Co.'s work of the same period.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Cut live in the studio with a full band, The Magnolia Electric Co. opens with the long, surging 'Farewell Transmission' and never really lets up, trading Molina's earlier hushed folk for Crazy Horse-scale electric guitar, organ and drums. 'I've Been Riding with the Ghost' and 'Just Be Simple' pair big, ragged choruses with Molina's still-bleak lyrics about ghosts and highways. It gave the band its next name and its widest audience, and is the obvious entry point into the whole catalog.
albums.lineage: Sounds deeply indebted to Neil Young and Crazy Horse's ragged guitar rock, and gave its name to Magnolia Electric Co., the band Molina led for the rest of the decade.
key_tracks: I've Been Riding with the Ghost

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Pyramid Electric Co. strips everything back to Molina alone with voice, guitar and piano, the quietest record he made under his own name. The title track unfolds as a long, slow piano meditation, and 'Long Desert Train' keeps the same patient, lonely pace. It is a deliberate come-down from the full-band Magnolia Electric Co. album released the year before, a private, unhurried companion piece.
albums.lineage: A solo counterpart released the year after The Magnolia Electric Co., returning to the hushed, voice-and-instrument minimalism of the earliest Songs: Ohia records.

albums.album: Who Will Walk in the Darkness with You?
albums.label: Delmore Recording Society
albums.description: Columbus, Ohio's The Black Swans build a spare, haunted folk-rock sound around Jerry DeCicca's cracked, weary voice, with violinist Noel Sayre's playing giving the songs an eerie, mournful edge. The band's debut is slow and hushed throughout, closer to a graveside hymn than to a rock record, sharing the same Midwestern gothic-folk atmosphere as Songs: Ohia. It is Molina-adjacent in tone and geography without being directly connected to his bands.
albums.lineage: A Columbus, Ohio band working the same haunted, Midwestern gothic-folk atmosphere as Jason Molina's Songs: Ohia, sharing scene and tone rather than direct collaboration.
key_tracks: Who Will Walk in the Darkness With You?

albums.label: Misra/Munich
albums.description: Will Johnson's second solo record continues the quiet, plainspoken songwriting of 'Murder of Tides', with a little more instrumental color layered around the acoustic core. It is unhurried and downcast, closer in mood to South San Gabriel than to Centro-matic's guitar rock. It reinforces Johnson's status as one of the steadiest, most prolific songwriters in the Denton/Magnolia orbit.
albums.lineage: Continues Will Johnson's stripped-down solo work alongside his ongoing Centro-matic and South San Gabriel output.
key_tracks: Just to Know What You've Been Dreaming

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Recorded live in Brussels while the band still toured as Songs: Ohia, this was the first release under the Magnolia Electric Co. name. Stretched-out versions of songs like 'The Big Beast' lean hard into Crazy Horse-style guitar jams. It documents the moment Molina's haunted folk band turned into a loud, loose country-rock outfit.
albums.lineage: Documents Jason Molina's pivot from the hushed Songs: Ohia sound toward Crazy Horse-scale guitar rock, a move that set the template for Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio albums.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: The first proper studio album under the Magnolia Electric Co. name, recorded with Steve Albini at Electrical Audio, pairs Molina's cracked baritone with a full touring band for the first time. Songs like 'Northstar Blues' and 'Give Something Else Away Every Day' move at a slow, heavy backbeat, closer to a bar-band Crazy Horse than the spare folk of earlier Songs: Ohia records. It reads as a bridge record, still carrying some of the older band's hush but built for a road-worn rock lineup.
albums.lineage: Extends Songs: Ohia's haunted folk into full-band country rock, cementing the Magnolia Electric Co. sound that Will Johnson's Centro-matic and South San Gabriel records run parallel to.
key_tracks: Give Something Else Away Every Day

albums.album: The Carlton Chronicles: Not Until the Operation's Through
albums.label: Misra/Munich/Houston Party
albums.description: South San Gabriel's most fully realized album pushes Will Johnson's quiet side project further into slowcore territory, all patient tempos, sparse arrangements, and pedal steel drones. The record keeps a hushed, worried tone throughout. It is the clearest bridge between the Denton scene and the slowcore sound of Low and Codeine.
albums.lineage: Pushes Will Johnson's South San Gabriel project toward a sound indebted to Low and Codeine, a quieter sibling to both Centro-matic and Magnolia Electric Co.

albums.label: Misra/Cooking Vinyl/Houston Party
albums.description: Fort Recovery pairs some of Centro-matic's biggest, most anthemic guitar rock ('Patience for the Ride') with the same weathered, plainspoken vocals Johnson had carried since the 1990s. It also got a UK release through Cooking Vinyl. It is loud, confident main-band Centro-matic, for fans of ragged Crazy Horse-style country rock.
albums.lineage: A high point of Centro-matic's Denton guitar rock, running parallel to Magnolia Electric Co.'s mid-2000s records.

albums.album: Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go
albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Released the same year as Magnolia Electric Co.'s full-band Fading Trails, this sparse solo record leans on plain acoustic guitar and Molina's voice, recorded close and quiet. Songs like 'It's Easier Now' and 'Alone With the Owl' keep the arrangements minimal so the lyrics about isolation and endurance carry the weight. It is one of the most purely singer-songwriter entries in Molina's catalog, closer to the folk end of his sound than to the band's rock side.
albums.lineage: Continues the solo, stripped-down thread running from Pyramid Electric Co. through Molina's later work, released as a quiet counterweight to the same year's full-band Fading Trails.
key_tracks: Let Me Go Let Me Go Let Me Go

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Assembled from several separate sessions, 'Fading Trails' is patchier and more fragmentary than its predecessor, mixing full-band rockers like 'Don't Fade on Me' with short, spare pieces. It captures Molina restlessly moving between studios and lineups in the years before Magnolia Electric Co. wound down.
albums.lineage: A transitional Magnolia Electric Co. record whose sessions were later collected whole on the 'Sojourner' box set, showing Molina's late-2000s method of recording in pieces across different studios and bands.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Baltimore's Arbouretum plays slow, heavy, guitar-drenched folk-rock in a Crazy Horse-scale mode, with Dave Heumann's baritone drawl riding over extended, fuzzed-out solos. The band's second album is closer to stoner-rock heaviness than to the alt-country twang of Centro-matic, but shares the haunted, guitar-forward Americana of the Molina/Magnolia catalog. It plays like a doom-tinged cousin to Neil Young's own Crazy Horse records.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Neil Young/Crazy Horse guitar lineage that also runs through Magnolia Electric Co., pushing it toward heavier, stoner-rock-adjacent territory from Baltimore.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: A limited wooden box set collecting three full albums (including the otherwise-unreleased 'Nashville Moon', produced by Steve Albini), a four-song EP, and a tour documentary, all drawn from the same 2005-2007 sessions that fed 'Fading Trails'. Because it gathers complete, otherwise-hard-to-find recordings rather than just repackaging an existing album, it functions as a genuine (if sprawling) entry in the discography rather than a reissue. It is for the committed listener who wants the full session-by-session picture of Magnolia Electric Co.'s mid-2000s work.
albums.lineage: Collects the same 2005-2007 Magnolia Electric Co. sessions that produced 'Fading Trails' in their entirety, including material otherwise unavailable, and stands as the fullest document of the band's road-band, Crazy Horse-indebted period.

albums.label: The Listening Party
albums.description: The Black Swans' second album, made before violinist Noel Sayre's death reshaped the band, keeps the same spare, mournful folk sound as the debut on songs like 'New Face' and 'Hope Island'. Jerry DeCicca's plainspoken, weathered voice stays the focus throughout, with minimal backing letting the songs breathe. It is a quieter, less-known cousin to the Songs: Ohia catalog, built from the same Midwestern small-town gloom.
albums.lineage: Continues The Black Swans' hushed, Midwestern gothic-folk sound, part of the same regional atmosphere (Ohio, small-town gloom) that produced Songs: Ohia.

albums.label: Misra/Cooking Vinyl/Houston Party
albums.description: A double album pairing a disc of loud Centro-matic guitar rock with a disc of quieter South San Gabriel material, 'Dual Hawks' makes explicit that Will Johnson is the same songwriter running both projects at once. The Centro-matic half stays true to the band's fuzzed-out sound, while the South San Gabriel songs slow things down into hushed, pedal-steel-laced country-folk. Taken together it is the clearest single portrait of Johnson's split musical personality.
albums.lineage: Unites Will Johnson's two parallel bands, Centro-matic (loud) and South San Gabriel (quiet), on one release, showing both halves of the Denton sound side by side.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Arbouretum's third album keeps the band's heavy, extended-jam approach to guitar rock with slightly more melodic songwriting on tracks like the title track and 'False Spring'. Dave Heumann's plainspoken baritone still anchors songs that stretch past five and six minutes, closer to a doom-folk take on Crazy Horse than to conventional alt-country. It is a strong mid-period entry in the band's catalog.
albums.lineage: Continues Arbouretum's heavy-guitar folk rock, which sounds indebted to Neil Young's Crazy Horse records and sits near Molina's electric work.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: The only proper collaboration between Jason Molina and Will Johnson trades the road-band roar of Magnolia Electric Co. for hushed, largely acoustic duets. Songs like 'All Gone, All Gone' and 'The Lily and the Brakeman' put the two songwriters' voices side by side rather than layered into a band mix. It is a quiet, weathered capstone to the whole Magnolia/Centro-matic orbit.
albums.lineage: Joins Jason Molina and Centro-matic's Will Johnson directly, making explicit the kinship between Songs: Ohia/Magnolia Electric Co. and the Denton scene.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Recorded with Steve Albini as a tribute to late Magnolia Electric Co. bassist Evan Farrell, 'Josephine' is the band's last studio album released in Molina's lifetime. It is quieter and more mournful than the road-band records around it, built on hushed strumming and Molina's weathered voice on songs like the title track and 'Whip-poor-will'. It works as a fitting, restrained close to the Magnolia Electric Co. catalog.
albums.lineage: Closes out Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio catalog as a memorial record for bassist Evan Farrell, before Molina's final years of illness.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: 'The Gathering' is Arbouretum's widest-reaching record, built on long, heavy guitar excursions like 'Song of the Nile'. Dave Heumann's baritone stays plain and unhurried even as the guitars pile up into extended, distorted jams. It is the clearest entry point into Arbouretum's Crazy Horse-scale sound.
albums.lineage: The fullest expression of the Baltimore band's heavy-guitar folk rock, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and sits near the Molina/Magnolia-adjacent V1 lane.

albums.label: Undertow Music Collective
albums.description: Centro-matic's penultimate album keeps the band's guitar-forward rock intact while sounding more settled and self-assured than the earlier, scrappier records. It came in the same stretch as the Molina and Johnson collaboration and carries some of that same weathered songwriting. It is late-period Centro-matic: still loud, still drawled, a band comfortable in its own long-running sound.
albums.lineage: Late-period Centro-matic, released as the band's Denton run wound toward its final album.

albums.label: Graveface Records
albums.description: A short set released during Molina's illness, Autumn Bird Songs gathers brief, plainly recorded songs like 'Heart My Heart' and 'The Harvest Law' that feel closer to sketches than to a full statement. It is quieter and more fragile than his earlier work, released on Graveface rather than his usual home at Secretly Canadian. For a small, committed audience it is one of the last pieces of new music Molina put out in his lifetime.
albums.lineage: One of Molina's final releases before his 2013 death, extending the hushed solo-acoustic mode of Pyramid Electric Co. and Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go into a briefer, more fragile form.

albums.label: Undertow Music
albums.description: Will Johnson's first solo album in eight years returns to the plain, weathered acoustic songwriting of his earlier solo records. It sits comfortably alongside his other 2010s work, a quiet counterpart to the louder Centro-matic albums.
albums.lineage: A 2010s continuation of Will Johnson's solo songwriting, running parallel to the final years of Centro-matic and his collaboration with Jason Molina.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Arbouretum's fifth album keeps the band's slow, heavy guitar-rock formula intact on tracks like 'The Long Night' and 'Renouncer', with Dave Heumann's baritone as unhurried as ever over extended, distorted jams. It moves at the same volume and pace the band had established since 'Rites of Uncovering'. Later albums like 'Let It All In' would keep the sound going.
albums.lineage: Closes Arbouretum's core lane-era run of Crazy Horse-scale Baltimore guitar rock, a sound the band would continue past 2013 largely unchanged.

albums.album: Take Pride in Your Long Odds
albums.label: Navigational Transmissions
albums.description: Centro-matic's final album wraps up nearly two decades of ragged, Crazy Horse-tilted Denton guitar rock. As a farewell record it plays like a summation of the band's whole run, from lo-fi 1990s beginnings to the more assured songwriting of its later years.
albums.lineage: Closes out Centro-matic's run as a band, the year after Jason Molina's death; in effect the end of the classic Molina/Magnolia-era Denton circle.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: A later Will Johnson solo record, released well after Centro-matic's 2014 breakup, keeps the same plainspoken, acoustic-centered songwriting he has carried since 'Murder of Tides'. It is quieter and more reflective than his band records, the sound of a veteran Denton songwriter still working the same hushed, weathered vein two decades on. It extends the Molina/Magnolia circle's aftermath well past the lane's core years.
albums.lineage: A post-Centro-matic Will Johnson solo record continuing the hushed, plainspoken songwriting he established in the Molina/Magnolia era.

albums.label: Thrill Jockey
albums.description: Released well past the lane's core years, Arbouretum's later album 'Let It All In' keeps the same slow, heavy guitar-rock sound the band established with 'Rites of Uncovering' over a decade earlier. Dave Heumann's baritone and the band's extended, fuzzed-out jams on tracks like 'A Prism in Reverse' show a band that has not changed its approach much since 2007. It is included here as a continuation of the same unbroken Crazy Horse-scale catalog rather than a new direction.
albums.lineage: A 2020 continuation of Arbouretum's long-running Crazy Horse-scale sound, unchanged enough from their 2007-2013 records to belong with the rest of their V1 catalog.

albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.description: Recorded in the 2000s but shelved until after Molina's 2013 death, Eight Gates was assembled and released by Secretly Canadian in 2020 as a posthumous studio album. 'Whisper Away' and 'Shadow Answers the Wall' sit in the same hushed, piano-and-guitar territory as Pyramid Electric Co., by turns unfinished-sounding and quietly devastating. It gave fans a final, previously unheard chapter of Molina's writing, released under his own name seven years after he died.
albums.lineage: A posthumous release of 2000s-era Molina recordings, closing out the catalog begun with Songs: Ohia's 1997 debut and continued through his solo and Magnolia Electric Co. work.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: A hushed, spare set built from historical fragments, including the Spanish Civil War setting of 'Teruel', matching Johnson's plainspoken, weathered voice to sparse guitar and occasional strings. It sits at the quiet, wounded end of his catalog, for listeners who like slow, patient songs.
albums.lineage: Continues Johnson's solo work after Centro-matic and his 2009 collaboration with Jason Molina (V1), in a quieter, more skeletal register.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Will Johnson (Centro-matic, South San Gabriel) sings in a craggy, weathered rasp over spare, atmospheric folk-rock built from acoustic guitar, brushed drums and low organ drones. It is unhurried, private-feeling songwriting, closer to a late-night confession than a rock record.
albums.lineage: Johnson recorded a joint album with Jason Molina (Molina and Johnson, 2009), a direct link to V1; this solo record carries that haunted, Crazy Horse-shaded Americana into a quieter register.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Diamond City is patient music with effortless hooks, leading with Will Johnson's weary voice and evocative lyrics over unhurried, largely acoustic arrangements. It is the sound of the same Denton songwriter who led Centro-matic still working the same plainspoken vein decades on.
albums.lineage: The most recent entry in Will Johnson's solo catalog, extending the Centro-matic/South San Gabriel/Molina and Johnson lineage.
